ch08 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Eberl reads Jax's Season 5 dilemma (Tara's ultimatum to leave SAMCRO or lose his family) through Aristotle's account of virtue as character cultivated by habituation in a polis. SAMCRO nurtures genuine virtues—Opie's selfless loyalty, courage under fire, the club's communal generosity toward Donna and Lyla—alongside vices like Clay's greed and Tig's lust, with the golden mean distinguishing Bobby's critical loyalty from Chuckie's obsequiousness and Juice's rash minefield charge. Fr. Ashby's fight to keep Abel in Belfast away from Jax's cycle of violence, and the contrast between Deputy Chief Hale's law-abiding ideals and Mayor Hale's self-serving development, illustrate Aristotle's claim that legislators and environments make citizens good or bad. The chapter concludes that Jax's very mix of virtue and vice—the 'savage' needed to head the table—may be what reform requires, at moral cost.

chapters.file: ch09 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Uses Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals to explain why viewers root for SAMCRO's criminals: the Sons embody master morality, the warrior virtues of strength, boldness, and reverence for worthy enemies—seen in Jax's elaborate trap that gets Jimmy O killed and Opie executes Stahl in the Season 3 finale, and in Clay sparing Marcus Alvarez. Agent Stahl personifies ressentiment: after Otto disfigures her she vows 'I'm gonna bury these assholes,' dressing revenge as justice and respecting no one, while principled 'good guys' like Potter and Deputy Chief Hale internalize the slave morality of equality and sympathy. The lambs-and-birds-of-prey passage frames our unease at Jax dismissing Tig's murder of an unarmed woman as 'collateral damage,' and the chapter ends by weighing whether a world without noble 'blond beasts' like Jax would be Nietzsche's tragedy.

chapters.file: ch10 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Takes Tig's misplaced revenge on Laroy—which kills Veronica Pope and triggers Damon Pope's burning of Tig's daughter and Opie's prison murder—together with the club's unconditional convoy rescue in 'To Be, Act 1' to ask whether loyalty is a virtue. It tests three accounts: the Aristotelian view (via Ladd's 'loyal Nazi is a contradiction') that only the virtuous can be loyal, which would deny that SAMCRO members can be loyal at all; the Humean view that loyalty is bigoted partiality; and the Kantian point that only the good will is unconditionally good, so loyalty can serve any wrongdoing. The chapter defends Ewin's line that loyalty is good in itself but issues in right action only joined with virtue, while the Stahl frame-up of Opie and Donna's death show the dark enforcement side—'rats deserve to die, end of story.'

chapters.file: ch11 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Puts Aquinas's Murder Principle—the private, intentional killing of an innocent is always murder—to the Men of Mayhem, arguing the Sons lack the public authority Aquinas requires to kill even the guilty. The show itself erodes the state/private line Aquinas needs: corrupt agents Kohn and Stahl, and the CIA's Romeo Parada running the Galindo Cartel, make the badge look like no moral credential at all. The Doctrine of Double Effect sorts the rest: Jax shooting first in self-defense, Tara's morphine for the dying Unser, and Juice's hypothetical land-mine sacrifice are merely foreseen deaths, while Jax syringing Clay or Juice's intentional hanging would be murder. The chapter concludes that even if Aquinas condemns the Sons, his questions about authority, innocence, and intention are exactly the ones the show forces on viewers.

chapters.file: ch12 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
ch13 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Reads John Teller's failed 'off the social grid' experiment through the human-nature debate: Mencius's seed of sympathy (even Tig recoils at Dante's dogfights) and Rousseau's naturally good man corrupted by society inspired J.T.'s Goldman-fed anarchism, while Mill and Xunzi counter that virtue is a victory over instinct. Hobbes supplies the real diagnosis—not innate violence but the logic of anarchy among free and equal rivals: competition (the Mayans blowing up the warehouse), diffidence (first-strike temptations against Zobelle), and glory (Jax unable to let the bike-sitting insult pass). Clay's rule that 'retaliation must be harsh and immediate' and the escalating Tig–Veronica Pope–Damon Pope–Opie bloodbath show deterrence fueling cycles of violence, so the only escape from the 'nasty, brutish, and short' fringe is the Leviathan's social grid.

chapters.file: ch14 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Argues that a motorcycle club is a Machiavellian regime in miniature: Jax's Season 3 fake betrayal of the club to Stahl—actually a set-up that shortens the crew's prison time and delivers both Stahl and Jimmy O to death—shows the prince's union of lion and fox in service of the club rather than himself. J.T. figures as a founder overcome by fortuna ('each savage event was a catalyst for the next... blood was every color'), lacking the virtu to impose his vision, while Clay wields deceit and force for mere egoism that Machiavelli would refuse the name of glory. Zobelle's self-description as a 'Machiavellian fool' flooding Charming with drugs, and Jax's admission that 'you can't sit in this chair without being a savage,' frame the chapter's question of whether manipulation and violence can serve a genuine common good.

chapters.file: ch15 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Explains what anarchism actually demands—rejection of external authority, voluntary association, and faith that people need no coercion to cooperate—and measures SAMCRO against it: the club's president, church votes, chain of command, and the impossibility of Jax negotiating an exit all betray Momma Anarchy. The individualist/collectivist debate inside anarchism maps onto J.T., who retreats to Nomad and Belfast when the collective disappoints his individualist ideal, versus Jax, whose commitment to family keeps him building the collective. Clay appears as the anti-anarchist 'stone-cold egoist' who rigs votes and kills suspected rats, and the chapter argues the experiment was doomed twice over: the founding Vietnam vets' military hierarchy, and the club's dependence on the capitalist society and state agencies (CIA RICO leverage) it rejects.

chapters.file: ch16 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Asks whether SAMCRO's gun suppliers, the Real IRA, are terrorists or freedom fighters, using Walzer's definition of terrorism as random killing of innocents to spread fear and his combatant/non-combatant distinction. The Irish Kings pass as freedom fighters—Kutz's three criteria of internal ordering (the hierarchy that has Sean Casey strangle the turncoat Cameron Hayes), just aims (a united Ireland), and target discrimination fit them—whereas Jimmy O, recruiting children as young as ten and attacking anyone with Loyalist sympathies, fails; his real motive being profit, Fr. Ashby concludes 'he's not a soldier anymore, just a gangster,' prompting the chapter's new category: thug. Fr. Ashby's own complicity in a church execution, redeemed by becoming a hostage so Abel can return to Jax, closes the moral ledger.

chapters.file: ch17 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Runs SAMCRO's conflicts with the Mayans, the Lobos Sonora, and the ATF through just war theory's jus ad bellum, focusing on right authority: Clay's dismissal of Salazar ('I don't recognize your bullshit MC') is exactly how Walzer would treat Clay's own war declarations. Walzer's analogy of the sovereign state to Tara shooting her home-invader Kohn grounds the right of self-defense in sovereignty, and the chapter tests SAMCRO against four features of statehood and six of nationhood—brothers as compatriots, the club's founding history obligating Jax, church votes, Charming turf, the Reaper tattoo, and self-determination—to crown it a 'mini-nation-state on wheels.' The catch is Clay's own admission that Sons are US citizens: the United States remains sovereign over them, leaving open whether sub-state nations like SAMCRO (or the Palestinians) can ever legitimately declare war.

chapters.file: ch18 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
ch19 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Uses SAMCRO's ink—Jax's full Reaper backpiece and John Teller memorial, Opie's portrait of Donna, Tig's marine 'Death Before Dishonor,' Juice's head tattoos—to argue that personal identity lives in the body, not just the mind. Descartes's cogito opens the 'I ink, therefore I am' framing but proves too thin to connect the thinking Jax to the tattooed body, so the chapter turns to Merleau-Ponty's claim that 'it is the body which points out, and which speaks': the tattoo makes the body itself the expression, and its meaning stays inexhaustible as the wearer changes. The Kyle Hobart episode—burned and cut for failing to black out his Reaper after expulsion—shows tattoos as identity claims the community can veto, making 'fire or knife' an enforced correction of a false statement about who he is.

chapters.file: ch20 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Reads SAMCRO as an unconventional community of faith through Durkheim's account of religion as a symbol system binding a moral community: Opie's wake in the chapel, the mugshot wall of martyred brothers, and the sacred Reaper logo, cuts, and clubhouse function as hierophanies, with the Mexican cult of Santa Muerte as proof that criminals can have genuine folk religion. Burkert's Männerbund thesis explains the MC's all-male ritual bonding, its suppressed aggression (Tig versus Kozik), and the inevitable subordination of wives like Donna to the club. The tragedy reads as Hamlet transposed—stepfather Clay murdered the father J.T. and seized the throne—and the club's tragic flaw is written into its own symbols: a faith whose central icon is the Reaper and whose orb bears the A of anarchy cannot hold together, since its sacred transgression of rules dissolves the very brotherhood it consecrates.

holes.name: Loyalty (partiality to one's own)
holes.what: Devotion to particular persons or groups because they are one's own rather than because of their qualities, raising the problem of whether such partiality can be virtuous or must lead to wrongdoing.
holes.why: Chapter 10 is entirely organized around whether SAMCRO's loyalty—enforced by death for rats and extended even to Tig's disastrous revenge—can be a virtue, debating Royce, Oldenquist, Ladd, Hume, and Ewin on the topic.

holes.name: Émile Durkheim
holes.what: French sociologist who redefined religion as a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things which unite into one moral community those who adhere to them.
holes.why: Chapter 20's entire reading of SAMCRO as a community of faith—Opie's wake, the sacred Reaper logo, cuts, and chapel—is built explicitly on Durkheim's Elementary Forms of Religious Life.

holes.name: The Sacred and the Profane
holes.what: The distinction that religious communities set apart 'sacred' things—forbidden to the uninitiated—that embody the group's collective spirit and identity.
holes.why: Chapter 20 argues SAMCRO's Reaper tattoo, cuts, clubhouse, and chapel are sacred objects whose policing (blacking out Clay's ink, fire or knife for Kyle Hobart) marks the community's boundaries.

holes.name: Männerbund (hunting origin of religion)
holes.what: Walter Burkert's thesis that religion and ritual originated in all-male cooperative hunting bands that ritually re-enacted hunts and sublimated male aggression.
holes.why: Chapter 20's 'MC and MB' section uses the Männerbund to explain SAMCRO's male bonding, hierarchy, rivalries like Tig and Kozik, and the subordination of family to the club.
